SYSTEMS PROGRAMMING AND MACHINE ORGANIZATION
Chapter 17 — Procedures and Calling Conventions
VERBATIM GRADUATE LECTURE TRANSCRIPT
Charles Dorner

SLIDE 1: Chapter 17 — Procedures and Calling Conventions

LECTURE NARRATION
A calling convention lets independently compiled functions exchange arguments, results, and control without knowing one another’s internal implementation. It specifies the state that must exist at a call boundary and what may change before return. Handwritten assembly must satisfy that contract just as compiler-generated code does.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, a calling convention lets independently compiled functions exchange arguments, results, and control without knowing one another’s internal implementation.

SLIDE 4: 17.1 call

LECTURE NARRATION
A near call transfers control to a target and places a return address on the stack. The return address identifies where execution should continue after the callee finishes. On the reference 64-bit convention, the pushed return address occupies eight bytes. The instruction itself does not allocate a complete source-level stack frame or save every register. Those are responsibilities handled by the caller and callee according to the ABI. A function can therefore be extremely small if it needs no local stack storage and changes no callee-saved register.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, a near call transfers control to a target and places a return address on the stack.

SLIDE 6: 17.2 ret

LECTURE NARRATION
A normal ret obtains the return address from the stack and transfers control there, advancing the stack pointer accordingly. It assumes the stack state has been restored to the expected return-address position. A mismatched push/pop sequence or corrupted return address can send execution to the wrong location. Stack canaries and other mitigations can detect or constrain some corruption, but they do not make an incorrect frame layout safe. Verify the stack pointer at each return path, especially when a function has early exits.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, a normal ret obtains the return address from the stack and transfers control there, advancing the stack pointer accordingly.

SLIDE 8: 17.3 Argument registers

LECTURE NARRATION
For ordinary integer and pointer arguments in the System V AMD64 ABI, the first six use %rdi , %rsi , %rdx , %rcx , %r8 , and %r9 . Additional arguments may use the stack. Floating-point and vector arguments use other rules and register classes, and aggregates require ABI classification. This simplified rule is enough for the scalar examples in this book. It is not sufficient for every structure return, variadic call, or C++ object interface. When interoperating with an unfamiliar signature, consult the full ABI and inspect a compiler-generated reference rather than guessing from the number of parameters. [ R4 ]

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, for ordinary integer and pointer arguments in the System V AMD64 ABI, the first six use %rdi , %rsi , %rdx , %rcx , %r8 , and %r9 .

SLIDE 10: 17.4 Return registers

LECTURE NARRATION
Ordinary scalar integer and pointer results commonly return in %rax . Some wider or aggregate results use multiple registers or caller-provided storage. Floating-point results commonly use vector registers such as %xmm0 under the applicable rules. The result type determines how the caller interprets the returned bits. Declaring an assembly function with the wrong C type can produce a mismatch even when the routine returns a sensible machine value. Keep the declaration and assembly contract together, including width, signedness, and any hidden storage assumptions.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, ordinary scalar integer and pointer results commonly return in %rax .

SLIDE 12: 17.5 Stack pointer

LECTURE NARRATION
The stack pointer tracks the active stack region used by calls and local storage. The callee must return with the caller’s expected stack position restored. Adjustments reserve or release space but do not initialize the bytes automatically. A stack allocation can be large enough numerically yet violate alignment or exceed the mapped stack. Dynamic-sized stack objects need careful bounds. Prefer heap or arena storage when input-controlled size could make stack use unbounded. A call chain’s total stack requirement includes every simultaneously active frame.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
Think of an address written on a note: the note can tell you where to look, but it does not prove the thing is still there or that you are allowed to use it.

SLIDE 14: 17.6 Stack frames

LECTURE NARRATION
A stack frame is the region and saved state associated with one active call. It may hold saved registers, spilled values, local objects, and outgoing arguments. Some leaf functions need no explicit frame allocation. Frame layout is a compiler and ABI matter, not a fixed translation of source declaration order. Optimization can reuse slots for nonoverlapping lifetimes or eliminate objects. Debugger displays reconstruct source concepts from machine state and metadata; an optimized-out variable is not necessarily missing from the computation.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, a stack frame is the region and saved state associated with one active call.

========================================================================================

SLIDE 16: 17.7 Stack alignment

LECTURE NARRATION
For the ordinary scalar calls used here, %rsp is 16-byte aligned immediately before call . The eight-byte return-address push means %rsp is eight modulo sixteen at callee entry, or equivalently %rsp + 8 is aligned. Additional alignment requirements can apply to particular stack-passed vector arguments. A callee that makes another call must account for its pushes and local allocation before doing so. One eight-byte push at entry changes the stack pointer from eight modulo sixteen to zero modulo sixteen, making it ready for a nested ordinary call. A second push would require another adjustment. Count bytes, not just source variables.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, for the ordinary scalar calls used here, %rsp is 16-byte aligned immediately before call .

========================================================================================

SLIDE 18: 17.8 Caller-saved registers

LECTURE NARRATION
Caller-saved registers may be overwritten by a callee. If the caller needs one of their values after a call, it must save the value in a preserved register or memory, or recompute it. The choice depends on lifetime and cost. An assembly routine cannot promise preservation accidentally and expect every future implementation to keep doing so unless that stronger promise is part of its interface. Callers should rely on the ABI contract, not on what a current disassembly happens not to modify.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, caller-saved registers may be overwritten by a callee.

========================================================================================

SLIDE 20: 17.9 Callee-saved registers

LECTURE NARRATION
A callee using %rbx , %rbp , or %r12 through %r15 must restore their incoming values before return. Saving them on entry and restoring them on exit is common, but optimized code can save only on paths that need them if unwind information and control flow remain correct. The saved value belongs to the caller. It is not the callee’s previous invocation state. Recursive calls therefore need independent preservation at each active level. A missing restore can corrupt a caller long after the callee’s own result appears correct.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, a callee using %rbx , %rbp , or %r12 through %r15 must restore their incoming values before return.

========================================================================================

SLIDE 22: 17.10 Local variables

LECTURE NARRATION
Local source objects may live in registers, stack slots, or no materialized storage at all. Address-taking can require an object to have addressable storage, but even then the compiler may optimize within the language’s observable behavior rules. A local array’s address must remain valid throughout every borrowed use. Passing it to a function that retains the pointer beyond return is unsafe. The calling convention transports the pointer correctly; it cannot extend the pointed-to object’s lifetime. ABI correctness and object-lifetime correctness are separate obligations.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, local source objects may live in registers, stack slots, or no materialized storage at all.

========================================================================================

SLIDE 24: 17.11 Recursive calls

LECTURE NARRATION
Each recursive invocation has its own logical parameters and local state. The machine commonly represents that state with repeated frames. If the recursion depth is d and each active frame requires roughly f bytes, stack use grows approximately with d*f , plus calling and alignment overhead. A base case is necessary but not sufficient for robustness. A valid but deeply nested input can still exceed the stack. Bound input depth, choose an iterative representation, or provide a resource-aware algorithm. Do not depend on tail-call optimization unless the implementation contract explicitly guarantees the needed behavior.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, each recursive invocation has its own logical parameters and local state.

========================================================================================

========================================================================================
SLIDE 26: 17.12 Function prologue

LECTURE NARRATION
A prologue establishes any required frame, saves preserved registers, and reserves local storage. A conventional sequence might push %rbp , copy %rsp into it, and subtract space. Many functions use a different or shorter sequence. Handwritten assembly intended to participate in debugging or unwinding should provide appropriate call-frame information directives. Those directives describe how to recover caller state; they are not executed instructions. A correct normal return path does not automatically imply correct exception or debugger unwinding through the routine.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, a prologue establishes any required frame, saves preserved registers, and reserves local storage.

========================================================================================

========================================================================================
SLIDE 28: 17.13 Function epilogue

LECTURE NARRATION
An epilogue reverses the frame setup: release local space, restore preserved registers, and return. Every exit path must satisfy the same caller-visible contract. A function with an error return still owes the caller its saved registers and stack alignment state. The epilogue is a useful review boundary. List what the function acquired or changed, then verify that each relevant item has been restored or intentionally returned. This resembles resource cleanup in C and C++ because both problems are about preserving invariants across a boundary.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, an epilogue reverses the frame setup: release local space, restore preserved registers, and return.

========================================================================================

SLIDE 30: Worked example — Preserving a value across a nested call

LECTURE NARRATION
The requirement is to compute mix(x, 5) + x , where mix(x, y) returns 3*x + y using unsigned arithmetic. The assembly caller must retain x across the call to mix . It uses the callee-saved %rbx , saving and restoring the caller’s original value. Companion listing: ch17/nested.S Companion listing: ch17/main.c At entry, %rsp is eight modulo sixteen. Pushing %rbx makes it zero modulo sixteen, satisfying the ordinary nested-call alignment. %rbx then holds 9 while mix is free to overwrite caller-saved registers. mix returns 32, the wrapper adds 9, and popping restores the original %rbx before returning 41.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, the requirement is to compute mix(x, 5) + x , where mix(x, y) returns 3*x + y using unsigned arithmetic.

SLIDE 31: Worked example — Preserving a value across a nested call — Deep Dive

LECTURE NARRATION
The requirement is to compute mix(x, 5) + x , where mix(x, y) returns 3*x + y using unsigned arithmetic. The assembly caller must retain x across the call to mix . It uses the callee-saved %rbx , saving and restoring the caller’s original value. Companion listing: ch17/nested.S Companion listing: ch17/main.c At entry, %rsp is eight modulo sixteen. Pushing %rbx makes it zero modulo sixteen, satisfying the ordinary nested-call alignment. %rbx then holds 9 while mix is free to overwrite caller-saved registers. mix returns 32, the wrapper adds 9, and popping restores the original %rbx before returning 41.

SLIDE 32: Worked example — Tracking a call frame

LECTURE NARRATION
Suppose a function needs 24 bytes of local storage but the ABI requires stack alignment at call boundaries. The compiler may round the stack adjustment upward, for example to 32 bytes, rather than allocate exactly 24. It also preserves any callee-saved registers it modifies. The frame therefore reflects ABI obligations as well as source locals.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, suppose a function needs 24 bytes of local storage but the ABI requires stack alignment at call boundaries.

========================================================================================
SLIDE 34: Worked example — Caller-saved versus callee-saved

LECTURE NARRATION
If a caller needs a value currently in a caller-saved register after invoking another function, it must arrange to preserve that value, perhaps by spilling it. A callee that modifies a callee-saved register must restore it before returning. This division lets callers and callees coordinate without knowing each other’s source code.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, if a caller needs a value currently in a caller-saved register after invoking another function, it must arrange to preserve that value, perhaps by spilling it.

SLIDE 38: Chapter Synthesis

LECTURE NARRATION
The chapter's central subject is procedures and calling conventions. Correct reasoning requires explicit assumptions, bounds, ownership, and interface contracts. Observed behavior is evidence about a run; it is not automatically a language or system guarantee. Use the worked examples and lab to test whether the model transfers to new cases.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true.
